demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
Going to or near the place where the event happened
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I should have protected others and I failed
I have failed in my most important role in life

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: For a trauma defined as accidentally causing serious injury to another, 'Avoid Perpetrator Cues' is hard to reconcile because it implies the patient was harmed by a perpetrator rather than being the agent who injured someone else. That is a direct mismatch with the trauma type.

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Humiliation' is not impossible after this trauma, but paired with the rest of the profile it lacks a clear link to the accidental-injury context; the dominant themes would more plausibly be guilt, responsibility, or fear of causing harm again. It is weaker than the perpetrator-cue problem but still clinically questionable here.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Body-focused shame is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another, unless there was also significant injury or disfigurement to the patient; no other selected items indicate patient bodily injury, making this appraisal clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used as distraction is not impossible, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other items emphasize guilt, threat vigilance, and cue-triggered distress related to the accident, whereas self-harm implies a severe affect-regulation strategy not supported elsewhere in the selected items. This strategy is therefore clinically poorly anchored in the presented formulation/profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, a burnt smell implies a fire/burning context that is not supported anywhere else in the profile. With no matching memory content or appraisal theme tied to smoke/fire, this trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'People are not what they seem' suggests interpersonal mistrust/paranoia, which is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile centered on guilt and failure to protect after accidentally injuring another person. It does not connect plausibly to the listed triggers or strategies and is not supported by any interpersonal threat content.

vignette:
The night of the performance, Marcus had felt the familiar surge of adrenaline as he launched into the partnering sequence. The music swelled, the stage lights were hot on his skin, and the dancer in his arms was a familiar weight. He had done this lift a thousand times. But a bead of sweat, a momentary shift in her balance, a fraction of a second where his grip faltered—he would never know the exact cause. What he knew, with a clarity that had not faded in the three years since, was the sickening lurch in his stomach as she fell. He heard the crack of her arm against the unforgiving stage floor, a sound that later became the only thing he could hear in a quiet room. She was a principal dancer, a friend, and he had dropped her. He had broken her.

In the weeks and months that followed, Marcus’s world contracted. He could not go back to the theater. The very thought of the rehearsal room, of the sprung floor where it happened, sent a cold panic through him that was worse than any physical injury he had ever sustained. He stopped driving altogether. It was not the cars themselves, but the sudden, unbidden image of a vehicle striking a pedestrian, a cyclist, anyone—the flash of an accident he had caused, projected onto every intersection. He would be standing on a street corner and see a car hesitate at a light, and his mind would supply the rest: the screech of tires, the body on the pavement. He would flinch so violently that his wife, Elena, began to drive him everywhere.

The music was the worst. A random song on the radio in a coffee shop could ambush him, the melody instantly transporting him back to that moment on stage. His throat would close, his hands would shake, and he would have to leave. He began to wear noise-canceling headphones even at home, a quiet act of desperation to control the auditory world around him. He had come to believe that his entire identity, the one thing he had been good at, the role of a partner who made others look weightless and beautiful, was a lie. He told himself that he had failed in the most fundamental duty of a dancer—to protect the person in his care. He would replay the fall in his mind, searching for the exact second he could have done something different, a micro-adjustment of his core, a stronger grip. He was certain that if he had just been a fraction more aware, a fraction stronger, he could have stopped it. The guilt was a physical weight in his chest, a voice that whispered he did not deserve to move through the world without pain.

His concentration shattered. He could not follow a conversation in a restaurant, his eyes darting to every doorway, every sudden movement. At home, he could not relax. Even in their quiet living room, with Elena reading beside him, his body was wired for a catastrophe that had already happened. Sleep was a battleground. He would lie in bed, his mind refusing to surrender its vigilance, replaying the event or simply scanning the dark for threats he could not name. He tried, with all his will, to push the memory away. He would say to himself, Don’t think about it. Think about anything else. But the effort to suppress the thought was itself exhausting, a constant, draining war.

The most painful consequence was the slow erosion of his marriage. Elena, a former dancer herself, tried to understand. But she could not follow him into the logic of his guilt. She would say, “It was an accident, Marcus. It happened.” But he knew, with a certainty that felt like the only truth he had left, that it was not an accident. It was his failure. He had stopped teaching, stopped even going to watch rehearsals. The living room became his whole world, a small, safe prison where he could control the stimuli, where no music played unexpectedly, where no one needed him to be strong.

He came to therapy because Elena had finally said, with tears in her eyes, that she could not watch him disappear. He came because he was afraid of what he might become: a man who had not only broken a colleague’s body, but had also broken his own life. He was terrified that there was no way back to the person he used to be, but he was even more afraid of the alternative—a future spent forever trying not to think, forever failing to forgive himself.
